analysis.one_liner: Charges hardrock mining companies fees, royalties, and cleanup bonds for extracting minerals from federal public land.
analysis.headline: The Hardrock Mining Reform Act of 1993 was referred to a House Natural Resources subcommittee in April 1993 and never received a vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the 1872 General Mining Law, companies mining gold, silver, copper, and other hardrock minerals on federal public land pay no royalty to the government and can patent — buy outright — the land they claim. This bill would have charged miners a $25 location fee and $100 annual maintenance fee per claim, imposed a 2% royalty on newly located claims, required fair market value payment for newly patented land, mandated reclamation bonds and environmental compliance, and created a grant program to clean up abandoned hardrock mines. It was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers would gain a share of mining revenue that today goes entirely to mining companies: two-thirds of new fees, royalties, and patent payments would go to the federal Treasury and one-third to the states where the mining occurs [S3]. People living near old mines would benefit from a new federal grant program to seal dangerous shafts, treat acid mine drainage, and reclaim land and water ruined by abandoned hardrock mines [S3]. Anyone who uses or lives near public land would gain from requirements that miners post reclamation bonds, follow federal and state environmental laws, submit approved operating plans, and accept quarterly inspections [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a $25 location fee and a $100 annual maintenance fee per mining claim, with fees waived for claimants holding 10 or fewer claims and reduced to $25 per claim for small holders, so the burden falls mainly on large operators; failure to pay voids the claim.

Imposes a 2% royalty on the value of locatable minerals produced from any mining claim located after enactment, with a review commission to study the royalty's effect on the industry, and directs two-thirds of receipts to the federal Treasury and one-third to the affected state.

Requires claimants patenting land after enactment to pay fair market value for the surface estate, limits use of patented land to mining-related purposes, and provides for the land to revert to the United States if it is used for unauthorized purposes.

Requires approved plans of operations for any mining that more than minimally disturbs the surface, compliance with federal and state environmental laws, quarterly inspections, fines up to $2,000 per day for violations, and financial guarantees covering the full estimated cost of reclamation.

Establishes an Abandoned Hardrock Mine Reclamation Program giving grants to states to seal abandoned shafts, control acid mine drainage, and restore land and water damaged by past mining, prioritizing protection of public health and safety, with annual appropriations capped at the prior year's federal receipts from the bill.

analysis.who_pays: Hardrock mining companies operating on federal land would pay for the first time: a $25 location fee and a $100 annual maintenance fee per claim (indexed to inflation), a 2% royalty on minerals from newly located claims, fair market value for the surface of any newly patented land, and bonds covering the full estimated cost of reclaiming land they disturb. Failure to pay the fees would void the claim [S3].

drawbacks.text: The 2% royalty applies only to mining claims located after the bill's enactment, so existing claims — the bulk of producing mines — would have paid no royalty, sharply limiting the new revenue.
The Secretary of Interior could reduce or waive the royalty whenever deemed necessary to promote development, giving an executive official wide discretion to shrink the public's take.

The royalty review commission's nine members would all be appointed by the Secretary from people with experience in the economics of the hardrock mining industry, raising the prospect of an industry-weighted review.

The bill's own findings make reform conditional on not harming mining employment, mineral supply, or the trade balance, language that frames any meaningful charge on the industry as potentially self-defeating.

A good-faith objection from mining communities: new fees and royalties could raise production costs in towns that depend on mining jobs, a concern the bill itself acknowledges by conditioning reform on protecting employment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefits — federal and state revenue from minerals taken from public land, cleanup money for abandoned mines, and reclamation bonds so taxpayers are not left holding the bill — come at the direct expense of mining companies that currently pay nothing for the minerals they remove. The design has real weaknesses: the royalty skips all existing claims and is only 2%, the Secretary can waive it, and the review commission is drawn from mining-industry economics, so the bill's revenue promise is softer than its headline. Even so, the core bargain — public resources yielding public revenue, and miners guaranteeing their own cleanup — plainly favors the public over a single industry, and the bill's modest small-claimer waivers show it was written to spare independent prospectors.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in a House Natural Resources subcommittee from April 1993 onward, was folded by reference into the broader mining reform bill H.R. 322, and died when the Congress ended without ever coming to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced April 7, 1993 by Rep. Bill Orton with Rep. Barbara Vucanovich and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on April 27, 1993, where it received no further action of its own.

On October 28, 1993 the record pointed to the broader mining reform bill H.R. 322, leaving H.R. 1708 without a vote of its own; the 103rd Congress ended January 3, 1995 without the bill reaching the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hardrock mining companies are better off: they kept mining federal land with no royalties, no per-claim fees, and no new reclamation guarantees, and they faced no fair-market-value charge when patenting public land. Taxpayers and people living with abandoned mine pollution gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Bill Orton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 7, 1993 and championed it in the House.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Vucanovich
for.what_they_did: Joined Orton as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: 2 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only additional support it attracted.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.role: House Natural Resources Committee and its Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 7 and sent it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources on April 27, where it sat without a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Hardrock mining industry
against.role: Gold, silver, and copper producers on federal public land
against.what_they_did: Fought the broader 1993 mining reform effort through lobbying and advertising campaigns arguing royalties would destroy mining jobs, as the broader bill H.R. 322 cleared the House but died in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Utah Democrat joined by two Nevada Republicans whose districts depend on mining; no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the partisan shape beyond sponsorship is unknown.

industries.industry: Hardrock mining companies (gold, silver, copper, and other locatable minerals)
industries.note: The bill would have ended the industry's free ride on federal land: new claims would carry a 2% royalty, annual fees, full reclamation bonds, and fair-market-value payment for patented land. Under the 1872 General Mining Law these companies pay no federal royalty at all, so the industry's gain in the status quo is money the public does not collect.

industries.industry: Land patent claimants converting public land to private ownership
industries.note: The bill would have required fair market value for newly patented land instead of nominal claim-patent prices, and would have restricted patented land to mining-related uses with reversion to the United States if misused.

The bill funds an abandoned-mine reclamation grant program that would create reclamation work, but it also requires quarterly federal inspections of mining operations, which the bill itself acknowledges could add costs.
